title: Catalase Test
principle: Catalase-positive organisms produce the enzyme catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas. Bubble formation upon adding hydrogen peroxide to a bacterial sample indicates this reaction.
purpose: Commonly used to distinguish catalase-positive genera (e.g. Staphylococcus, Micrococcus) from catalase-negative genera (e.g. Streptococcus, Enterococcus) among Gram-positive cocci, as one step in a broader identification workflow.

procedure.instruction: Using a sterile loop or wooden applicator stick (avoid an iron/nichrome loop or blood-agar-derived colonies, both of which can cause false positives), transfer a small amount of an isolated colony onto a clean glass slide or into a test tube.
Add a drop of 3% hydrogen peroxide directly onto the sample.

interpretation: A positive result indicates the organism produces catalase; a negative result indicates it does not, under the test conditions used. This is one differentiating character, not a full identification.
precautions: Avoid transferring colony material from a blood agar plate, since residual red blood cells (which contain catalase) can cause a false positive.
Avoid an iron- or nichrome-containing loop, which can catalyze a false-positive reaction with peroxide.
limitations: A weak or delayed bubbling can be ambiguous and should be repeated or confirmed.
Contamination with catalase-positive organisms from surrounding media can produce a false positive.
